d.title: One method and one operator is the whole protocol
d.caption: The fastest way to understand what the framework is doing is to write the part that matters, and it is smaller than it looks. **A protocol needs one method; composition needs one operator.** Define `invoke` on a base class and `__or__` to return a sequence that calls each member's `invoke` in turn, and `prompt | model | parser` already works. Everything else in this course is built on those two lines.

nodes.label: The sequence calls each in turn
And everything else builds on it

d.title: The test of an interface: add a type nobody anticipated
d.caption: Add a component the original author never planned for — a retry wrapper — and see how much existing code has to change. **The answer is none.** `Retry` wraps anything and is wrapped by anything, because the only thing it needs to know about its neighbours is that they have `invoke`. That is the whole payoff, and it is why `with_retry`, `with_fallbacks` and `with_config` can ship as methods on the base class: **each one is just a wrapper that satisfies the same protocol.**

nodes.label: So wrappers can be base-class methods

d.title: Six methods rather than one, and the idea is unchanged
d.caption: The library's contract is the hand-built one plus five more methods, and **each addition is a capability the uniformity makes free rather than a new concept.** `batch` is many inputs with bounded concurrency; `stream` is incremental output *through the whole chain*, not just the model; the `a`-prefixed half is async; and `with_config` attaches callbacks, tags and runtime values per call. Anything implementing them composes with anything else that does.

nodes.label: invoke
nodes.sub: the same as the hand-built one

nodes.label: ainvoke / abatch / astream
nodes.sub: the async half of every method

d.title: A class per role, so something downstream can pattern-match on it
d.caption: A conversation is a list, and each entry has a role. **The framework gives each role a class rather than a dict key**, which is what lets a parser or a graph pattern-match on it later — `isinstance(m, ToolMessage)` is a branch you can write, and `m["role"] == "tool"` is a string comparison you can misspell. The fourth is the one with real structure: a `ToolMessage` is tied back to the call that produced it by `tool_call_id`.

nodes.label: AIMessage
nodes.sub: the reply, or a tool it wants to call

nodes.label: So you can branch on type

d.title: The model receives a flat list of messages and nothing else
d.caption: Templates, partial variables, few-shot examples, message placeholders and chains are **all machinery for producing one thing**: a flat list of messages. Three quite different constructions produce byte-identical lists here. **The model does not receive your variables, your template, your chain structure or your intentions** — which is why the single most useful debugging move in this course is to render the prompt and look at the list.

nodes.label: All three produce the same list
The model sees only that
nodes.sub: not the structure that built it

d.title: batch is 5.8x the loop, and max_concurrency is the dial
d.caption: `batch` runs the inputs **concurrently against a thread pool** and returns results in input order, which on this workload is **0.726 s down to 0.126 s — 5.8×**. The third row is the one worth knowing: `max_concurrency=2` gives 0.365 s, so the parameter is a real throttle rather than a hint. Which makes it the control you reach for when the provider's rate limit is the binding constraint rather than your own patience.

d.title: If a tutorial imports a *Chain class, reach for the modern equivalent
d.caption: The pre-LCEL named chain classes are deprecated, **they still fill tutorials and interview questions**, and knowing the modern equivalent for each is worth more than it should be. The rule of thumb is mechanical and the reason is concrete: **you get streaming, async, batching and tracing for free, none of which the legacy classes support** — so porting is not a style preference, it is how those four features become available at all.

nodes.label: None of which the legacy classes have
nodes.sub: so it is not a style choice

d.title: A missing variable is loud; an unapplied partial is silent
d.caption: A partial fills a variable at construction rather than at the call site, and removes it from `input_variables`. **The failure mode is asymmetric and that is the thing to carry.** A *missing* variable is a loud `KeyError` at invoke time. A partial you intended to apply and did not is **silent** — the literal text `{tone}` goes to the model, which will usually produce a plausible answer, so nothing fails and nothing is logged.

steps.code: a partial you forgot to apply

d.title: Where a prompt grows without anyone deciding that it should
d.caption: `MessagesPlaceholder` splices a list of messages into the template, which is how conversation history enters a prompt — and **it is the single most common place for a prompt to grow with nobody choosing to grow it.** The growth is perfectly linear at **+52 characters a turn** here, which is the shape to recognise: nothing spikes, nothing errors, and by turn eight the prompt is **ten times** what it was at turn one.

d.title: Every example is in every request, forever
d.caption: Few-shot examples are not a special mechanism — `FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate` renders each one as a human turn followed by an AI turn, **producing an invented conversation the model treats as precedent**. The cost is structural: **ten examples at thirty tokens each is three hundred tokens on every call for the lifetime of the service.** Which is the argument for a semantic example selector: pick the k most relevant per query, trading a retrieval step for a permanent prompt tax.

nodes.label: Each example becomes a turn pair
For the lifetime of the service

d.title: Whether your chain works depends on which side the model puts its chattiness
d.caption: `Here is the review:` followed by valid JSON **raises**. The same JSON followed by `Hope that helps!` **parses fine.** The parser looks for the first JSON-shaped span and reads to the end of it, so **leading prose derails the scan and trailing prose is never reached.** The consequence is uncomfortable: whether your chain works is a property of the prompt and the model version rather than of your code, so **a chain can be stable for months and break on a model update.**

nodes.label: The scan starts on the prose
So it is a property of the model
Stable for months, broken by an update
nodes.sub: and nothing in your repo changed

d.title: Truncation is repaired instead of reported
d.caption: `JsonOutputParser` uses a **partial** JSON parser because it has to — it is the same parser used to stream, where incomplete input is normal rather than an error. On a non-streamed response that means truncation is **silently repaired**. A rating truncated to `8.` parses as `8`; a title truncated mid-word parses as the truncated word; an unclosed array is closed. **Every one is a plausible value of the right type**, so no downstream validation catches it either.

d.title: A forgiving parser is not a more robust parser
d.caption: There is a tempting intuition that a forgiving parser is more robust, and these rows show the opposite. **The marker stays attached** — `'1. a\n2. b'` becomes `['1. a', '2. b']` — and a numbered or bulleted list is exactly what a model produces when asked for a list unless told otherwise. And `'a, b, and c'` yields **`'and c'`**. The parser never raises, so a downstream loop iterates over wrong-shaped data and **the bug surfaces somewhere else entirely.**

d.title: A parser and its format instructions must travel together
d.caption: `get_format_instructions()` returns text the chain injects into the prompt — **the parser telling the model what shape to produce**, and it is explicit about the failure modes above, fences and preambles included. Which makes the practical consequence sharp: **swapping a parser without re-running the prompt is a silent change.** The prompt still asks for the old shape, the new parser expects a different one, and **nothing in the type system connects them.**

nodes.label: The prompt asks for the old shape
nodes.sub: the parser expects a new one

nodes.label: Nothing in the types connects them
So move them as a pair

d.title: Repair is cheap; the deciding factor is whether the failure is visible
d.caption: At a 5% parse-failure rate a fixing parser costs **1.05 calls per request on average** — cheap enough that cost is not the deciding factor. The deciding factor is **visibility**: a fixing parser converts a loud exception into a silent extra call, so **a parse-failure rate that was an alert becomes a cost line nobody reads.** Which is why the first row wins on a different axis: with `with_structured_output` there is nothing to parse, so there is no failure to make visible.

d.title: The data arrives in a field that was never a string
d.caption: `with_structured_output` **does not ask for JSON and then parse it.** It binds your schema as a **tool definition**, the model emits a tool call, and the call's arguments are validated into your type. The model's text output is empty and **the data arrives in a structured field that was never a string** — which is why every failure mode in 1.4 is simply absent here rather than mitigated: there is no text to scan, no fence to strip and no truncation to repair.

nodes.label: The model emits a tool call

d.title: A Field constraint is both the request and the guarantee
d.caption: This is the argument for putting constraints in `Field()` rather than in prompt text. **"Rate out of ten" in a system message is a request.** `Field(ge=1, le=10)` is **both** — a request, because it appears in the schema the model sees, **and** a guarantee, because the value is checked before it reaches you. One declaration does both jobs, and the prompt-text version does only the first and gives you no way to know when it was ignored.

nodes.label: "Rate out of ten" in the prompt
In the schema the model sees
nodes.sub: so it is still a request

nodes.label: And checked on the way back
nodes.sub: so it is also a guarantee

d.title: Three mechanisms behind one line of code
d.caption: `with_structured_output` picks one of three, and **which one you get decides what you are guaranteed.** Tool calling is strongest and needs a tool-calling model. JSON mode guarantees **valid JSON but not necessarily *your* schema** — the distinction that matters, because a valid object with the wrong fields passes the parser and fails your code. And prompt-and-parse works anywhere and is the weakest, with every failure mode from 1.4 attached.
cells: the schema bound as a tool

cells.text: valid JSON, but not YOUR schema

d.title: A Literal does two jobs from one declaration
d.caption: It **appears as an enum in the tool schema**, so the model is told the allowed values, **and** it is enforced on the way back, so a model that invents a fourth category **raises rather than widening your data.** Writing "answer positive, negative or neutral" in the prompt does only the first — and the third row is what that costs you. `Optional` is the companion: an omitted field arrives as `None` rather than as an absence you have to test for.
